seo.title: Karmic tail 15 17 11 compatibility: The Devil, The Star, Strength
seo.description: Karmic tail 15 17 11 compatibility: The Devil, The Star and Strength — love on terms, truth without a mirror, passion held in hand, via Gogol's Christmas Eve.

title: Karmic tail 15-17-11 in compatibility: how a couple holds the devil by the tail
short: The karmic tail 15-17-11 in compatibility is The Devil, The Star and Strength. The couple enters its task through love on terms: "I love you — if you prove it" (The Devil, entry to the task). It goes through the task by way of a night in which the pretty picture loses its value and it becomes clear what each of them really feels (The Star, middle of the task). And it learns the main lesson: not to climb onto each other's necks, and not to let passion ride on the necks of both, but to hold their own devil by the tail (Strength, main task). Gogol wrote this plot down almost word for word, in "Christmas Eve".

sections.h2: The 15-17-11 tail in compatibility: the three cards in brief

ul: **Entry to the task — 15, The Devil.** What the couple wants together: to belong to each other completely. Its common language is the language of conditions and proof. The wish is strong, and that is exactly why it also holds the couple back: where love is bought, it soon gets tested too.

**Middle of the task — 17, The Star.** How the couple travels the path: through a trial by shop window — gifts for show, comparisons, the image of a "beautiful couple" — and through the moment when the window goes dark and the plain truth is all that is left.
**Main task — 11, Strength.** What the couple has to learn: power without pressure. Not to settle who is riding whom, but to hold together what used to hold them — passion, jealousy, pride.

paragraphs: The tail does not predict events and passes no verdict on the union. It shows where the couple stumbles and what works for it once it sees this. What follows is the evidence: in the numbers, in the books of Waite and Wen, and in one Christmas tale in which all three cards stand in their places.

sections.h2: The riddle: a middle no single person can have
paragraphs: The 15-17-11 tail has an oddity that shows only in the arithmetic. In a personal matrix the middle of the tail always equals the sum of its ends: the entry plus the main task. If 15-17-11 were one person's tail, its middle would be 15 + 11 = 26 → 8 — **Justice**. But a couple's points are counted differently: each one is the sum of the matching points of two personal matrices. The couple's middle is built from the partners' middles, and it comes out as 17 — **The Star**. That is why the order 15-17-11 is impossible as a personal tail: it happens only between two people.

The swap is telling. Justice is the card of the scales; Waite calls it "the moral principle which deals unto every man according to his works". And in the same breath he sets apart something else — gifts which "we have them or have not, and their presence is as much a mystery as their absence". "The law of Justice," he adds, "is not however involved." One person's logic would lead from The Devil to Strength across the scales: tit for tat. The couple travels it through The Star — through what is not weighed.

That is the hidden plot of this tail. Such a couple is drawn to live by the scales: to test, to prove, to keep score, to set conditions. And everything that works for it works when the score is cancelled.

The tail is rare: about one couple in 955 (0.105%), 82nd place out of the 97 couple tails. And none of its three cards belongs to either of the two. All such couples are made of just two combinations of personal tails: 6-8-20 + 9-9-18 (94%) and 6-14-8 + 9-3-21 (6%). The Devil at the entry is built in both cases from one partner's Lovers and the other's Hermit — from choice and from solitude. Neither The Devil, nor The Star, nor Strength appears in anyone's personal tail: all three cards are born only between the two.

There is an even finer detail. The scales are in the couple after all — in the personal tail of one partner: in 94% of such couples Justice stands in the middle of that partner's tail (6-8-20), in the rest at its end (6-14-8). The couple brings its scales along. But in the middle of the couple's tail they are added to The Hermit, 9 + 8, and give The Star: one partner's scales and the other's solitude together become what is not weighed. This does not mean that either of the two is bargaining: a personal tail is a different calculation with different roles. It is only about what the numbers are made of.

sections.h2: Entry to the task — The Devil: a night when everything is for sale
paragraphs: "Christmas Eve" (1832, the second volume of "Evenings on a Farm near Dikanka") opens with a theft. Gogol is quoted here from George Tolstoy's 1860 translation unless marked otherwise. A witch gathers stars from the sky — "In a short time the witch had got a whole sleeveful of them." The devil grabs the moon, tosses it from hand to hand "like a peasant who has taken a live coal in his hand to light his pipe", and hides it in his pocket. He has "only one night more" left "for walking about the world", and he is taking revenge on the blacksmith Vakula for a painting on the church wall: the Apostle Peter, "at the Day of Judgment", driving the evil spirit out of hell. The Moon and the Day of Judgement — this is where Gogol begins. And from these same two cards, The Moon and Judgement (18 + 20 = 38 → 11), the main task, Strength, is built in 94% of couples with the 15-17-11 tail.

From there on, everything is arranged like a bargain. Oksana is not yet seventeen; she stands for an hour before a little mirror in a tin frame and argues with it: "No, I see very well that I am not at all beautiful!" — and at once: "No, I really am pretty! and how pretty! how beautiful!" Vakula is forging her a chest — "The iron I used for binding it! I did not use the like even for the centurion's tarataika" — and tries "to snatch a kiss". She pushes him away: "thy hands are harder than iron". And when her friend Odarka turns up in new gold-trimmed boots, Oksana names her price in front of everyone. The price is the Tsaritsa's own slippers, cherevichki, which the 1860 translation calls boots: "I call all of you to witness, that if the blacksmith Vakoola brings me the very boots which the Czarina wears, I pledge him my word instantly to marry him."

All of Dikanka is bargaining. In Solokha's sacks sit the village elder, the parish clerk and Chub, and "every one thought that Solokha nodded to him alone"; Chub, finding a rival in a sack, says what any owner would say: "and I thought that I was the only one." The devil, once he is riding the blacksmith, first of all demands paperwork: "thou knowest well that nothing can be done without contract." And he offers exactly what Vakula wants: "No later than this very day Oxana shall be ours!" Vakula answers with The Devil's formula in its purest form: "on this condition I am ready to be thine."

This is what The Devil means at the entry to a couple's task. It is not a vice and not an evil plan, but a wish the two share: to belong to each other completely. "Ours", "thine", "my word" — such a couple has a strong common language, and it is the language of ownership. It gives heat, passion, a feeling of "us against the world". Lisovskaya sees a real upside in this energy too: such couples can talk about their desires openly and accept each other's dark sides. But the entry to the task sits on the line of tasks, and the same wish turns into resistance: instead of "I want" comes "prove it", instead of a talk an iron-bound chest, instead of a request a contract. The object of the deal proved so memorable that Tchaikovsky, reworking his opera "Vakula the Smith" (1874), named the second version simply "Cherevichki", "The Slippers" (1885).

In a couple today the cherevichki take many forms. "If you love me, you'll move in." "If you're serious, you'll introduce me to your parents." An expensive present that matters not in itself but as evidence. A holiday that turns into an exam. Jealousy that keeps accounts. None of these scenes means the couple is bad. They mean the two share a strong wish — and so far have no language for it except conditions.

sections.h2: "The devil on his back": one's own devil, not a stranger
paragraphs: In despair Vakula goes to Fat Patsyuk, a former Zaporozhian Cossack who, as the blacksmith timidly puts it, "hast the devil among thy friends". Dumplings leap into the sour cream and into Patsyuk's mouth by themselves — pleasure without lifting a finger. Asked to show the way to the devil, he drops: "He who has got the devil on his back has no great way to go to him." Vakula does not understand. The reader already knows: the devil is sitting in a small sack on the blacksmith's back. Vakula himself heaved that sack onto his shoulders on his way out of the cottage, saying: "I think I put my instruments into it."

This may be the most important clue for the 15-17-11 couple. Its Devil does not come from outside — neither as a rival nor as a temptation. The couple carries it itself and takes it for its own tool: jealousy passes for care, testing for serious intentions, a condition for pride. Wen writes that The Devil card "does not necessarily mean the Seeker is entirely to blame." In the couple this shows in the numbers: The Devil is not in the personal tail of either of the two. It is not "his" and not "hers". It is shared, and the sack on the back is shared too.

Such a sack is heavy to carry. Vakula complains: "Some time ago, with one hand I could bend and unbend a copper coin, or a horse-shoe; and now, I cannot lift a few sacks of charcoal." And he asks what anyone in a couple with this tail might ask: "How is it that thoughts come into one's head against one's own will?" Among Waite's meanings for Strength reversed stands this very word — weakness — and next to it, discord. The couple's strength goes not into love but into hauling its devil around.

sections.h2: Middle of the task — The Star: the mirror and the dark
paragraphs: The middle of the tail is how the couple travels from the wish to the task. In Gogol it is a journey in the literal sense: a night flight to St Petersburg on the devil's back. How the blacksmith got there belongs to the main task, below. At first Vakula is frightened; then he "began to laugh at the devil". "All was bright in the sky. A light silvery mist covered the transparent air. Everything was distinctly visible" — even "how some stars, gathered in a group, played at blind man's buff". The night that began with stolen stars puts them back in the sky in the middle. Waite, by the way, begins his list of meanings for The Star not with hope but with "Loss, theft".

But the first thing that meets the blacksmith at the end of the flight is a shop window. Petersburg is "all in a blaze": an illumination, "all the houses looked at him with their innumerable fire-eyes", in the palace ladies "in silk gowns with long trains" — in Gogol's Russian, with "long tails" — and the blacksmith "was dazzled with the glitter of gold, silver, and precious stones". Before the Tsaritsa he does what he swore off that evening. Back then he dreamed of telling the Tsar: "I'll have no precious stones, no golden smithy, no, not even the whole of thy realm—give me only my Oxana!" Now he asks for the slippers: "Gracious Lord! if ever my wife had such boots to wear!" The Tsaritsa laughs: "This artlessness pleases me exceedingly."

Meanwhile, in Dikanka, the main thing is happening. Oksana, who spent the whole evening at the mirror, cannot sleep: "Now, tossing about in a bewitching nakedness that the darkness of the night hid even from herself, she scolded herself almost aloud; now, growing quiet, she resolved to think of nothing — and kept thinking. She was burning all over; and by morning she was head over heels in love with the blacksmith" (my translation; the 1860 version softens the nakedness into "bewitching attitudes"). The mirror showed her a face. The dark, in which she cannot see even herself, showed her a heart.

This is how The Star runs through the 15-17-11 couple. In its shadow side it is the shop window: a relationship lived for other people's eyes; gifts that get measured; comparisons — "Thou art happy, Odarka, to have a suitor who can make thee such presents"; ultimatums. Lisovskaya describes the shadow of The Star in a couple as a beautiful wrapping with nothing inside and a habit of seeing the partner as a fan rather than a person. In its light side it is the same radiance, only real: the rare case, she writes, when the pretty picture is the truth. The middle of the tail is the passage from one to the other: a night in which the mirror is useless, and so for the first time it is possible to see what is inside.

Next day the deal cancels itself. Vakula walks in with the slippers: "they are the very boots which the Czarina wears." Oksana waves her hands: "No, no, I do not want the boots!" — and then: "I'm fine without them…" (my translation) — "She could speak no more, and her face turned all crimson." The condition announced before witnesses has been met, but love came before the slippers: at night, when the blacksmith was thought lost and could bring nothing. The scales of Justice, which would sit in the middle of one person's tail, are replaced in the couple by The Star: a gift is not weighed. Wen calls The Star a card of "giving more than the Seeker receives". And Gogol ends the scene with a line the mirror could never earn: "Never yet had she been so marvellously handsome."

sections.h2: Main task — Strength: who rides on whose neck
paragraphs: The devil springs out of the sack and "sat upon the blacksmith's neck". He whispers into the right ear about friendship, into the left about money, into the right again about Oksana. The blacksmith agrees, the devil "began to indulge his joy in springing about on the blacksmith's neck" and demands a signature in blood. "Well, stop, let me take a nail out of my pocket," says Vakula, "and putting his hand behind him, he suddenly seized the devil by his tail." The sign of the cross — and "The devil grew as docile as a lamb." Without letting go of the tail, "the blacksmith sprang on his back".

The beast in this scene is one and the same. Only the rider changes. A minute ago the devil was riding the blacksmith; now the blacksmith is riding the devil. Russian has an exact idiom for this — "to sit on someone's neck", that is, to make them carry one — and the main task of the 15-17-11 couple reads first of all through it. In its shadow side, Strength is a contest over who rides whom: who sets the conditions and who meets them, who laughs and who is laughed at, whose truth counts more. Lisovskaya describes such a couple as a struggle for leadership in which each holds to their own truth and the two speak different languages. In Gogol this struggle comes to fists: the blacksmith steps into the porch "with the firm intention of giving vent to his wrath by breaking the bones of the first man who should come in his way" and, failing to recognise Chub in the snowstorm, shoves Oksana's father out of the door.

What Vakula does not do with the devil matters. He does not kill him and does not drive him off. Nor does he take what the devil offered — "Oxana shall be ours", a person delivered ready-made, without her will. The blacksmith orders something else: "Carry me on your back this minute, do you hear? Carry me like a bird!" (my translation; the 1860 version has "Take me a ride on thy back directly"). Tamed passion does not vanish — it carries. To Petersburg, to the Tsaritsa, to a deed of one's own. That is the light side of Strength: the energy that bent horseshoes and threw Chub out of the door now carries.

Waite, discussing "Transcendental Justice, the counter-equilibrium of the scales, when they have been overweighted so that they dip heavily on the side of God", gives advice that seems written for this scene: "to use loaded dice when you play for high stakes with Diabolus." Vakula plays exactly so. He pretends to look for a nail to sign with, while his hand goes for the tail. He has no arguments against the deal — only a gesture that cancels it.

True Strength comes to Gogol's hero the next day, and without any devils. At the first cockcrow Vakula gives the devil three blows with a stick, sleeps until midday and goes to Chub. He lays a new cap, a belt and a whip before him and falls at his feet: "There, take this scourge, whip me as much as thou wilt! I give myself up." Chub, "to make himself still more important", gives him three strokes. The devil got three blows — the blacksmith takes three. The strongest man in the village, the one "who bent copper coins between his fingers, as if they were so many buckwheat fritters", hands the whip to someone else himself. And with Oksana he is different now: that evening he tried "to snatch a kiss"; next day he "took her hand" and kissed her "gently".

For the 15-17-11 couple this is the main task read in its light side: power that does not press. Being able to hand over the whip — not out of weakness, but because there is no longer any need to prove who is stronger. Asking and listening to the answer instead of grabbing. Wen puts it plainly: "the Seeker cannot use brute force to exercise will over others; the Seeker must use gentle, subtle influence." Lisovskaya sets such a couple a simpler, more everyday task: from the very start, to say what each of them likes and dislikes, and to show feelings openly — then conditions are no longer needed.

sections.h2: Death at the centre: the blacksmith buried by rumour
paragraphs: In 93.9% of couples with the 15-17-11 tail the centre of the couple's matrix is 13, Death; in the remaining 6.1% it is 22, The Fool. The couple's centre is its shared atmosphere, what happens between the two when nobody is watching. In the tale this atmosphere has a scene of its own. While the blacksmith flies to Petersburg, Dikanka buries him. "I'll go and tell about the blacksmith having hanged himself," an old woman decides; the weaver's wife swears: "He is drowned! I'll swear to it, he's drowned!" The village elder sighs: "So much for the blacksmith! He was here, and now nothing is left of him!" — and adds: "How strong he was himself!" Next day Chub does not know what to marvel at most, "whether at the blacksmith being once more alive".

What dies here is not a man but a game. Oksana falls in love not with the blacksmith bringing slippers but with a blacksmith who is no more — on the night when he owes her nothing. Death at the centre of these couples is an atmosphere in which something has to end so that something else can begin: an old script, an old role, an old score. Lisovskaya sees in this energy at a couple's centre the ability to accept changes in a partner and move on, and in its shadow side, emotional swings. Gogol has the swings too: "She does not love me—well, God be with her!" — and a few lines later, "his every thought was bent on Oxana alone."

Wen notes that The Star "appears chronologically in the Major Arcana after a great deal of pain: The Hanged Man, Death, The Devil, and The Tower." In this couple The Devil stands at the entry and Death at the centre, so The Star in the middle of the tail ends up exactly where it belongs: after the end of the old game.

One caveat. "I'll go and drown myself" is, in Gogol, a lover's comic hyperbole. In life a threat of self-harm is not a plot for reading cards. If it is meant seriously, the call to make is to 112 or a psychologist, not to a matrix reading.

sections.h2: What Waite saw: tails, nakedness and a lion already tamed
paragraphs: The cards on the site have their own drawings, which differ in places from the Waite–Smith deck. But Waite's book contains three details of the images that read like a commentary on the tale.

**The Devil.** Waite's two chained figures have tails: "The figures are tailed, to signify the animal nature, but there is human intelligence in the faces." Gogol's devil is built in a similar way: "In front, it was just like a German", but "viewed from behind", the provincial advocate, "so much was its long pointed tail like the skirt of our dress-coats". The tail is what passion has behind it and cannot see itself. That is where it gets caught.

**The Star.** The woman on Waite's card is "entirely naked", and "for the majority of prepared minds", he writes, she is "the type of Truth unveiled". On Christmas Eve Oksana travels this road literally: from a little mirror in a tin frame to a nakedness that even she cannot see.

**Strength.** Waite stresses that his design differs from the usual ones in one point only: "her beneficent fortitude has already subdued the lion, which is being led by a chain of flowers." There is no struggle on the card — it ended earlier. And in one aspect, the lion "signifies the passions, and she who is called Strength is the higher nature in its liberation". Gogol has the same: after the sign of the cross there is no fight and no chase, only a devil "as docile as a lamb" and the blacksmith on his back. Wen writes of Strength that "the meek lamb will prevail over the open-mouthed lion"; in Gogol, the beast itself becomes the lamb.

sections.h2: How the 15-17-11 tail looks in a couple's life

ul: **The slippers.** One of the two sets a condition that cannot be met without a feat: "prove it", "earn it", "do it the way other people do". The other rushes to meet it and silently keeps a bill for the feat. Both call it love, and both get tired.
**The sack on the back.** Jealousy, checking up and old grievances, carried around for years and called care. Both find it heavy, and neither understands why: "but I'm already doing everything".

**The mirror.** The couple thinks a great deal about how it looks from outside: photos, gifts, celebrations for other people's eyes, comparisons with friends. And meanwhile the two do not tell each other the main thing.
**The neck.** Decisions about money, housing and relatives turn into a contest: whoever gives way has lost. Mockery instead of a request, an order instead of a question.

**A night without a mirror.** A quarrel, a separation, a long pause — and suddenly each of them can see what the other means to them. Sometimes after such a night a couple starts speaking a different language.

sections.h2: What changes the plot: how to hold the devil by the tail

ul: Say "I want" instead of "prove it". A wish said out loud is The Devil's light side; a condition in place of a wish is its shadow.

Check with one question: is this a gift or a payment? If a payment — for what, and who set the price. Lisovskaya advises such couples not to buy love with money and expensive presents; cherevichki are a purchase too.
Leave the other the right to say "no" without punishment. A strength that cannot bear refusal is not yet Strength.
Do not keep double books: who gave way how often, who owes whom. Keeping score in this couple is the first sign that the scales have moved back into the middle of the tail in place of The Star.
Do not grab — not a kiss, not a decision, not being right. Take a hand.
Call one's own devil by its name: jealousy is jealousy, fear is fear, pride is pride.

paragraphs: Gogol ends the tale not with a wedding but with a painting. Having performed public penance, Vakula painted the church choir "green, with red flowers running over it", and on the wall "which is to your left when you step into the church" he painted "the devil in hell" with "such an odious face that no one could refrain from spitting, as they passed by". Mothers brought crying children to the picture: "Look! is he not an odious creature?" — "and the children stopped their tears, looked sideways at the picture, and clung more closely to their mother's bosom." The devil has not gone anywhere. He hangs on the wall, where everyone can see him, and carries no one any more — he only frightens and amuses. This is the strong version of the 15-17-11 tail: a couple that knows its devil by sight, keeps him in view and does not let him climb onto its neck. Lisovskaya ends her chapter on The Devil in a couple with a thought Gogol showed in a whole tale: **nobody belongs to anybody**.

sections.h2: The couple's values: the world, the home and penance
paragraphs: "The couple's values", the spiritual purpose, in couples with this tail is one of three cards: 21, The World, in 51.8%; 3, The Empress, in 31.3%; 12, The Hanged Man, in 16.9%. Gogol's epilogue, read as our interpretation rather than a rule, holds all three. The Hanged Man is the penance the blacksmith "performed" before painting the church. The Empress is the home: a passing archbishop asks, "Whose cottage is this, so highly painted?", and the answer comes from Oksana, standing at the gate "with an infant in her arms". The slippers, incidentally, were also handed out by an empress — Catherine. And The World is the whole journey: from Dikanka to Petersburg and back, around the whole world, which at the start of the tale was measured by the words "on that side of Dikanka and on this side of Dikanka" (my translation).

Wen calls Strength "a foreshadowing of what it will take for a Seeker to reach Judgement and The World". In half of the couples with the 15-17-11 tail The World is exactly what stands in the values: the main task leads to what this union exists for.

A couple's tail is counted from the points of two personal matrices: each point of the couple is the sum of the partners' matching points, reduced to 22. The example is the couple 11.02.1976 and 07.08.1976.

The partners' personal tails are 9-9-18 and 6-8-20. If the couple's middle were counted the personal way, from the ends, it would be 15 + 11 = 26 → 8, Justice. But it is built from the partners' middles, 9 + 8, and the result is The Star. "The couple's values" here is 21, The World. And on the "Image of the couple", where it shows how others see the couple, these two have 18 — The Moon. The very one Gogol's devil stole.

ul: N. V. Gogol. "Christmas Eve" ("Noch pered Rozhdestvom", 1832); Russian text after the Complete Works in 23 volumes, vol. 1 (Moscow: IMLI RAN, 2001); English quotations from "The Night of Christmas Eve", translated by George Tolstoy (Cossack Tales, 1860), except where marked "my translation".
A. E. Waite. The Pictorial Key to the Tarot (1910; 1922 reprint).
Yuliana Lisovskaya. "Matritsa sudby: sovmestimost" ("The Destiny Matrix: Compatibility", 2024).
P. I. Tchaikovsky. "Vakula the Smith" (1874) and the second version of the opera, "Cherevichki" (1885), libretto by Yakov Polonsky.

faq.q: How can a couple tell it has the karmic tail 15-17-11?
faq.a: Two dates of birth are needed. A personal matrix is built for each, then the matching points are added: entry of the tail to entry, middle to middle, main task to main task; a sum above 22 is reduced by adding its digits. The compatibility calculator does this by itself. The 15-17-11 tail comes only from the personal tails 6-8-20 and 9-9-18, or 6-14-8 and 9-3-21.

faq.q: Why is there no such tail in a personal matrix?
faq.a: In a personal matrix the middle of the tail is the sum of the entry and the main task. For 15 and 11 that is 26 → 8, so one person would have Justice in the middle. In a couple the middle is built from the partners' middles, and it comes out as 17. There are no other couple tails made of these three numbers either: the order 15-17-11 is the only one.

faq.q: Does the 15-17-11 tail mean bad compatibility?
faq.a: No. The method gives no compatibility percentages and passes no verdicts. The Devil at the entry speaks of a strong wish and a language of conditions, not of vice; Strength in the main task speaks of what the couple is learning. The tail shows where the union gets stuck and what opens it up.

faq.q: Who in the couple is Vakula, and who is Oksana?
faq.a: Neither — and both. Gender is not part of the calculation, and the roles of the tail are not split into "his" and "hers". It happens that each of the two is in turn the one who sets the condition, the one who rushes to meet it, and the one with the sack on their back.

report: In Gogol's "Christmas Eve", love begins with a price announced in public. "I call all of you to witness, that if the blacksmith Vakoola brings me the very boots which the Czarina wears, I pledge him my word instantly to marry him," Oksana tells her friends — the "boots" being the Tsaritsa's own slippers, cherevichki. A few pages later the devil offers the blacksmith the same deal from the other side: "No later than this very day Oxana shall be ours!" Vakula answers, "on this condition I am ready to be thine" — and the devil at once demands paperwork: "nothing can be done without contract." The couple's karmic tail 15-17-11 — The Devil, The Star and Strength — is built like this tale. The couple enters its task through love on terms, goes through it by way of a night in which the pretty picture loses its value, and learns the main lesson: **not to let its devil climb onto its neck, but to hold it by the tail**.

report.h3: A devil the couple carries itself

report: The Devil at the entry to the task is neither a vice nor someone else's temptation. It is a wish the two share: to belong to each other completely. Such a couple has a strong common language, and it is the language of ownership: "ours", "thine", "my word". It gives heat and a feeling of "us against the world". But the same wish turns into resistance: instead of "I want" comes "prove it". "If you love me, you'll move in." A present matters not in itself but as evidence. A holiday turns into an exam, jealousy keeps accounts.

Gogol shows where this devil comes from. Desperate, Vakula asks Fat Patsyuk to show him the way to the evil one and hears: "He who has got the devil on his back has no great way to go to him." At that moment the devil is sitting in a small sack on the blacksmith's back — Vakula heaved it onto his shoulders himself, saying: "I think I put my instruments into it." The 15-17-11 couple is the same: **its Devil is not a third party or an outside enemy, but something the two carry themselves and take for their own tool**. Jealousy passes for care, testing for seriousness, a condition for pride. Such a sack is heavy to carry. "Some time ago, with one hand I could bend and unbend a copper coin, or a horse-shoe; and now, I cannot lift a few sacks of charcoal," complains the strongest man in the village.

report.h3: A middle where the scales should have stood

report: This tail holds an oddity. One person with the same ends of the tail would have Justice, the scales, in the middle. The couple has The Star there. Waite describes Justice as "the moral principle which deals unto every man according to his works", and in the same breath sets apart gifts which "we have them or have not". Such a couple is drawn to live by the scales: tit for tat. And everything that works for it works when the score is cancelled.

Gogol runs The Star through his whole night. The blacksmith flies to Petersburg, "everything was distinctly visible", and at the end of the road waits a shop window: a city "all in a blaze", ladies "in silk gowns with long trains", and he "was dazzled with the glitter of gold, silver, and precious stones". In its shadow side a couple's Star is exactly that window: a relationship for other people's eyes, gifts that get measured, comparisons, ultimatums. Meanwhile in Dikanka, Oksana, who spent the whole evening at the mirror, lies awake, "tossing about in a bewitching nakedness that the darkness of the night hid even from herself" — and "by morning she was head over heels in love with the blacksmith". She fell in love while the village was saying he had drowned, when he could bring her nothing. **The mirror showed a face; the dark showed a heart.** Next day the condition has been met — and is no longer needed: "No, no, I do not want the boots!" A gift is not weighed. "Never yet had she been so marvellously handsome."

In Gogol the threat to drown oneself is a joke. In life a threat of self-harm is not a plot for reading cards: if it is meant seriously, the call to make is to a local emergency number or crisis line, or to a psychologist.

The central scene of the tale is the couple's main task. The devil "sat upon the blacksmith's neck" and demands a signature in blood. The blacksmith promises to fetch a nail, and "putting his hand behind him, he suddenly seized the devil by his tail." The sign of the cross — and "The devil grew as docile as a lamb", while "the blacksmith sprang on his back". The beast is the same; only the rider changes. In its shadow side Strength in such a couple is a contest over who rides whom: who sets the conditions, who meets them, whose truth counts more. In its light side it is what Vakula does: he does not kill the devil and does not take the Oksana it offered him "ready-made", but orders: "Carry me like a bird!" **Tamed passion does not vanish — it carries.**

The next day Strength comes without any devils. The blacksmith lays a whip before Chub: "whip me as much as thou wilt! I give myself up." The man "who bent copper coins between his fingers, as if they were so many buckwheat fritters" hands the whip to someone else himself. And with Oksana he is different: that evening he tried "to snatch a kiss"; next day he "took her hand" and kissed her "gently". Power that does not press is the ability to ask and listen to the answer instead of grabbing.

report.h3: A devil on the church wall

report: The tale ends not with a wedding but with a painting. On the church wall Vakula painted "the devil in hell" with "such an odious face that no one could refrain from spitting, as they passed by", and mothers brought crying children to it. The devil has not gone anywhere — he hangs in plain view, known to everyone by sight, and carries no one any more. This is the strong version of the 15-17-11 tail: saying "I want" instead of "prove it", leaving the other the right to "no" without punishment, keeping no score of concessions, calling jealousy jealousy and fear fear. Lisovskaya ends her chapter on The Devil in a couple with a thought Gogol showed in a whole tale: **nobody belongs to anybody**.

unit.meaning: Your task is not to climb onto each other's necks but to hold your shared passion in hand: say “I want”, not “prove it”.
